strengths: The proposed transfer of information from source code and comments into an LLVM representation encoder is technically plausible and addresses an identifiable audience in program analysis and code representation learning.

The evaluation spans four downstream tasks and reports promising improvements, including function-name accuracy of 33.41 versus RoBERTa’s 29.41 and summarization BLEU-4 of 34.36 versus GraphCodeBERT’s 32.43. Ablations and a CodeT5 extension broaden the investigation.
The pipeline diagrams and equations communicate the high-level approach, and the manuscript supplies dataset counts, several training settings, and a public link for code and data.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central POJ-104 evaluation is inconsistent with the stated learning task. Section 2.3 describes supervised classification, while Section 3.2 and Table 2 specify disjoint sets of 64 training, 16 development, and 24 test classes. Ordinary supervised classification does not explain prediction of these unseen classes, yet Section 4.2 reports classification metrics across 104 classes. Specify whether this is retrieval, classification, or another protocol, define the metrics and evaluation populations, and provide corresponding results. This affects Tables 3, 7, and 8, including the main ablations.

Necessary: The experimental domain does not substantiate the broad claims about stripped executable binaries. Inputs are compiler-generated LLVM IR, and Figures 7–8 retain informative function, global, and type names. Such IR is not trivially interchangeable with representations recovered from stripped executables, contrary to the introductory footnote. Either restrict the claims to compiler-generated LLVM IR or evaluate the claimed executable-binary setting with documented lifting and identifier handling.

Necessary: Evaluation independence and target provenance need clarification. The relationship between the AnghaBench pretraining holdout, downstream train/development/test partitions, and reported validation/test scores is unclear in Sections 3.2 and 4.3. Document checkpoint selection, overlap handling across the GitHub-derived datasets, and which partition produced each result. Identify the summarization reference source explicitly; if references are CodeT5-generated, qualify what agreement with those references establishes.

Necessary: The experiments do not isolate the claimed benefit of interpolation and staged training. PCL receives 10 pretraining epochs, whereas the full model receives 30 or 70. Stating that PCL converged does not establish that the additional stages, objectives, and training budget have been disentangled. Use appropriately matched controls or narrow the component-level attribution. Repeated-run or paired uncertainty estimates are also relevant to small improvements, such as the 0.43-point reverse-engineering exact-match difference over GraphCodeBERT.

Necessary: The headline conclusions about human versus synthetic comments exceed the evidence. Table 7 reports MAF1 of 38.19 with synthetic comments, 37.40 without comments, and 3.06 with human comments. This shows a modest synthetic-comment increment and a severe failure in one human-comment configuration. Length distributions alone do not establish that verbosity, implementation detail, or stylistic variation caused that failure. Document comment extraction, paired-sample coverage, training controls, and stability; provide controlled evidence or restrict the conclusion to the tested configuration.

Necessary: Text-overlap metrics and selected examples do not establish the claimed semantic correctness of summaries or reconstructed programs. No execution, equivalence, or systematic human assessment is reported. Figure 7 also undermines its accompanying interpretation: GraphCodeBERT’s “Unloads the mutex” conveys essentially the same meaning as CONTRABIN’s “Unloads a mutex,” despite the assertion that competing summaries miss the functionality. Add validation appropriate to the semantic claims or narrow them to reference-text similarity. Table 6’s mixed results also require qualifying blanket outperformance claims.

Necessary: Method and result reporting contain consequential inconsistencies. Figure 3 feeds concatenated embeddings into the interpolation network, whereas Equations 8 and 10 use their sum; descriptions also differ on which modalities are interpolated or anchored. Resolve these differences and specify the actual pretraining configuration and downstream decoder construction. Section 5.1 incorrectly labels relative percentage reductions as point differences: Table 7’s MAF1 drops are 0.79, 2.85, and 6.97 points, not 2.07, 7.46, and 18.25 points. Together with the evaluation issues, these prevent the current manuscript from satisfying TMLR’s evidence and usable-communication criteria.
Optional: Quantitative neighborhood-quality measurements for the embedding visualizations and runtime or memory measurements would improve interpretation and practical guidance.
